pitch.short: I spent six years at Pinewick Paper & Print in Larchmont Falls, starting as a marketing assistant and ending as campaigns lead, selling reams, envelopes and ring binders to people who think paper is paper. I also film a weekly reel about a local shop, so I try most ideas on my own page before I put a client's money behind them.
why_hire: Six years at one regional paper company, rising from assistant to campaigns lead over a team of four, which taught me what a brief looks like once the warehouse has to pack it.
I launched a recycled paper range through 48 independent stationers: 4.2 million impressions over four weeks, with 31% of the opening month's orders placed on a stationer's own code.
At Tallow & Twine Stationers I tested handwritten postcards against branded email for a notebook refill plan and cut the cost of each reorder by 22%.

about.intro: I grew up in Larchmont Falls and studied communications at Ashgrove College, where I ran the student paper's advertising desk and sold more space than the editor wanted. I joined Pinewick Paper & Print as a marketing assistant in 2019 and stayed six years: first writing catalogue copy and mailers, then running the campaigns for the whole regional line under a manager, Gordie Pruitt, who believes any problem can be solved with an acronym on a whiteboard. In 2022 I began Larchmont Lunchbreak, a weekly reel on one local shop, which now has 38,000 followers. I came to Halden School of Management in 2025 to move into brand roles where I own the budget as well as the message.
about.now: Filming a weekly Ironby edition of Larchmont Lunchbreak, playing Tuesday-night five-a-side and writing Line Break, a weekly teardown of one regional print ad.

glow-creators.context: In March 2024 Pinewick launched Evergreen, a recycled copy paper, as the lead product of its spring catalogue. Recycled paper ads mostly show a tree and a white stack, and Pinewick's previous launch mailers had a 0.9% response rate. Gordie Pruitt's first idea was a billboard headline built on the acronym R.E.A.M.
glow-creators.problem: Office buyers suspect recycled paper will jam their printers, and they make that call at the shop counter, not on a website. We needed a display a shopkeeper could put up in five minutes, showing the paper itself, and looking nothing like the usual green advert.
glow-creators.my_role: Campaigns Lead, owned the idea, the stationer brief and the launch plan
what_i_did: Tested the idea first on two shops and in the Pinewick lobby: a sheet held to the window light shows the fibre texture, which looks better than a white stack.
Picked 48 independent stationers in Larchmont Falls, Ironby, Cresswell, Hobbs Landing and Marlow Heath by the repeat orders on their last two years of accounts, not by shop size.
Drafted a single-page brief asking for three photos and no script, plus a banned-word list including 'eco-friendly' and 'guilt-free'.
Held back 40% of the paid budget for 72 hours, then put it behind the six window displays that were being shared most.
Built the weekly tracker of impressions, shares and stationer-code orders that sales and marketing reviewed every Monday, with Marla Finch checking that her accounts were credited correctly.

decisions.choice: 48 independent stationers instead of one chain
decisions.why: The same budget reached 48 different high streets, and the stationers' own customers trusted them more than any ad.

decisions.choice: Show the sheet against the light
decisions.why: Shops that showed the fibre against the window got more shares than the ones with a perfect white stack, so every shop was asked to keep that shot in.

decisions.choice: Keep 40% of the paid budget in reserve for three days
decisions.why: We did not know which shops would take off. Waiting three days let us back the displays people were already sharing.

results.note: organic and boosted, first four weeks
in the first 19 days, Pinewick trade portal

glow-creators.learned: The plain window photos taken on a shop counter got a 4.2% share rate, against 1.1% for Pinewick's polished studio images.
glow-creators.next: Run the same idea for envelopes and binders: a counter display that lets buyers feel the weight, which is where the range loses to cheaper imports.

pav-patrol.context: I started Larchmont Lunchbreak in 2022 to practise filming and editing in my own time. It covers one Larchmont Falls shop a week, and since 2025 one Ironby shop as well.
pav-patrol.problem: Local pages mostly post a shopfront and a discount code. Owners told me they hated being marketed at, and every post looked the same, so I wanted something people would pass on because of the owner, not just the shop.
what_i_did: Fixed the format: a runtime below 40 seconds, the owner's name and opening year on screen from frame one, then a single line spoken by the owner.
Filmed every reel with a phone and a pocket gimbal in roughly an hour, then edited it in DaVinci Resolve over Sunday breakfast.
Recorded each reel in a spreadsheet: the hook, the duration, the kind of shop and a week of views, saves and shares.
Accepted paid work from 2023 under one rule: a sponsored reel only after four shop reels, and never any sponsor inside a shop reel.

decisions.why: Owners loosened up on camera and posted the reel on their own pages far more often after I dropped the grading.

decisions.choice: Lead with the owner, not the shop front
decisions.why: My own tracking sheet showed owner-first reels earning 2.4 times the shares of shopfront-first reels.

results.note: a corner café on Mill Lane, Larchmont Falls
a bakery supplier, a bike courier and a tea brand

pav-patrol.learned: On a small account, shares count for more than views: people who arrive through a share tend to stay, and explore-page viewers rarely do.
pav-patrol.next: A shared map of every shop I have covered, which followers keep asking for, and an Ironby series built the same way.

twt-creator-test.context: Tallow & Twine Stationers launched a notebook refill plan in early 2026. It sold well to people who walked into its shops, but slowly to online customers, who make up most of its new buyers.
twt-creator-test.problem: The branded refill email had a 1.9% reorder rate, and the cost of each online reorder in Ironby and Cresswell was well above the team's target.
twt-creator-test.my_role: Brand Marketing Intern, designed the test and wrote the postcard brief
what_i_did: Went through 400 customer reviews and receipt comments to see how buyers described the notebooks; 'lies flat' and 'does not bleed through' appeared most often.
Produced 18 postcard versions, each carrying a short hook lifted from those comments and signed by a named shop assistant.
Set up the test with the customer care lead: postcards and branded email sent to matched lists, with the same offer and the same refill page, for three weeks.
Followed every step from open and scan through basket to reorder in a single sheet, and handwrote two batches of the postcards myself.
Gave the marketing head the readout together with a proposal to shift 30% of the email budget into postcards.

decisions.choice: Use buyers' words as the hook
decisions.why: The brand's own copy dwelt on paper weight, whereas buyers first mentioned how a page behaves, and those hooks led from week one.

decisions.choice: Same offer and matched lists for both arms
decisions.why: Otherwise a difference in results might have come from the lists rather than from the postcards.

twt-creator-test.learned: The best postcards were the plainest. A two-line note from a named person beat the ones with a full-colour product picture.
twt-creator-test.next: Test the same hooks on the packing slip inside every online order, where the brand has not yet used a named person.

dabba-film.context: Back in 2022 Pinewick commissioned a film to open the back-to-school season for its Everyday notebooks. As Brand Executive on the account I spent five weeks with the creative director, the art director and a production house.
dabba-film.problem: Parents were the audience, and nobody likes a notebook advert, so the story had to give a parent a real reason to care about one particular page.
what_i_did: Scripted 90 seconds about a father who phones a stationery shop once it has shut, leaving answering-machine messages that describe his daughter's ideal notebook.
Wrote the father's messages as short, slightly muddled instructions, such as "The green one, with the lines. She'll know."
Developed the script alongside the creative and art directors through five weeks of drafts, each one read aloud by Tilly Brandt as a sound check.
Attended both days of the shoot alongside the production house.

decisions.why: We never see the father. His messages carry both the product and the bond with his daughter, and that is how the film stayed within 90 seconds.

decisions.choice: Set it in a shop after closing time
decisions.why: A dark shop and a ringing phone made the notebook feel like the most important object in town, without anyone stating it.

dabba-film.learned: One short line, phrased the way people actually speak, outdid every product claim, and I have written that way ever since.

cloud-kitchen-rebrand.context: During term 1 at Halden School of Management I headed a four-person team on a live brief for Parkside Supplies, which runs four school supply shops in Ironby and takes most of its orders through a web catalogue.
cloud-kitchen-rebrand.problem: The chain listed products under codes like NB-A5-R80-T3, and its photos were taken on a phone. Product-page conversion on the online store was 2.9%.
what_i_did: Gave 38 products names that state what they are and who they suit, such as "Sunday Planner Pad, one page per week" and "Ledger Book, the one accountants argue about".
Designed the chain's new Sharp & Square identity in Figma and Canva.
Reshot the product photos for the online catalogue.
Tracked product-page conversion for six weeks after the new listings went live.

decisions.choice: Rename the products before redesigning the logo
decisions.why: Shoppers on a web shelf read names well before they register a logo, so names offered the biggest room for improvement.
The chain could check it daily, and it told us straight away whether the new names and photos did their job.

results.note: one identity across all of them

cloud-kitchen-rebrand.learned: On an online shelf the product name does the selling, so names and photos are where a retail rebrand should start.

brandstorm.context: Two Halden School of Management classmates and I entered the 2026 Halden Cup, and I fronted the pitch. Six weeks stood between us and the national round.
brandstorm.problem: The aim was an idea a stationery maker could pilot with neighbourhood shops in small towns, with the shopkeeper as the recommender, and we needed evidence that shopkeepers would take it on.
what_i_did: Interviewed 36 shopkeepers in Larchmont Falls and Ironby before the national round.
Worked out the idea as a team: refill stations for ink and notebook inserts inside neighbourhood stationery shops, with the shopkeeper recommending each refill.
Planned a pilot in Larchmont Falls and Ironby with 20 shops, where the shopkeeper recommends the refill, refills the customer's pen or book at the station and posts a photo of the refill.
Made the slides in Figma and the interview log in Google Sheets, then delivered the pitch in the national round.

decisions.why: In our plan the shopkeeper suggests the refill at the counter and posts the photo, so the recommendation comes from someone the customer already trusts.

decisions.choice: Talk to shopkeepers before writing the deck
decisions.why: Our 36 interviews showed whether shopkeepers would sacrifice counter space for a refill station, the point on which the entire proposal rested.

brandstorm.learned: The interviews supplied the proof behind the pitch. Counter space, not slide polish, decided whether the plan could work.

steps: ink and inserts, at the station
visual.note: Pilot plan: Larchmont Falls and Ironby, 20 shops. Built on 36 shopkeeper interviews.

copy-that.context: Since 2024 I have published Line Break, a LinkedIn newsletter that dissects a regional brand's print ad every week.
copy-that.problem: My aim was a post that a busy marketer can read in a minute and act on, so each issue covers a single ad under three fixed headings.
what_i_did: Set a fixed shape for every issue: the headline, who it was meant for, and the one change I would test.
Pick a regional print ad each week, draft the post in Notion and design the cover in Canva.
Publish to LinkedIn weekly, with 64 issues out so far.

decisions.why: Covering a single ad let each post stay brief enough for the feed.

decisions.choice: Finish on the change I would test
decisions.why: It turns a critique into something a brand team can actually try on Monday.

copy-that.learned: 'Who was this headline meant for?' is now the first thing I ask of my own copy.

mu-fest.context: In 2025 I led marketing for the Larchmont Falls Print & Paper Fair, organised by the Halden School of Management marketing club and a team of six.
mu-fest.problem: We had five weeks and $4,800 to fill a two-day trade fair with buyers from schools and offices across the region.
what_i_did: Spent the bulk of the $4,800 on a local ambassador at 40 schools and offices instead of paid ads.
Gave each school and office its own referral code printed on a tote bag, so we could see which ones brought people.
With the club's six members I ran Instagram posts and WhatsApp codes, logging registrations per code in Google Sheets.

decisions.why: On $4,800 overall, we spent where buyers would hear about the fair from a person in their own building.

decisions.choice: One referral code per school or office
decisions.why: It revealed the source of each registration while the campaign had time left to run.

mu-fest.learned: With a code for each building, judging the spend was easy, because we saw what worked early enough to react.
